# Build with TypeSafe

TypeSafe makes units of AI intelligence usable like programming primitives: small
judgments you can compose into larger capabilities. Its **System One models** return
fast, focused judgments that software can consume directly. **Jev** is TypeSafe's
flagship and first System One model. It understands natural language and returns
typed answers and probabilities rather
than generating text or reasoning explanations. Code owns the workflow; the model
supplies programmable common sense where ordinary code needs semantic understanding.

## Read the live docs

**The live TypeSafe docs are the source of truth. Read them as part of the task.**
This skill gives direction; the docs carry current concepts, prompting guidance,
API contracts, SDK usage, models, limits, and worked examples.

- Start with the [documentation index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt) to discover
  relevant pages and cookbooks. Use targeted reads rather than loading the entire site.
- Mintlify serves Markdown by appending `.md` to a page path, for example
  [how to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md).
  Follow links from the index; convert extensionless documentation page links to
  `.md` when useful. Resolve relative links against `https://docs.typesafe.ai`.
- Before writing an integration, read the current API or chosen SDK page and the
  question guidance relevant to the design. For a new workflow, also inspect the
  closest cookbook: it often shows a better decomposition than a generic classifier.
- If the index is unavailable, use the direct links below or the site's navigation.
  If Markdown fetching fails, try the normal page. If live access is unavailable,
  use available local docs or installed SDK types, state that limitation, and avoid
  inventing version-dependent details.

| Task | Start here; follow the relevant details |
| --- | --- |
| Understand the programming model | [System One](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/system-one.md), [building guide](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md) |
| Explore what to build | [Use-case map](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/use-case-map.md), then relevant cookbooks from the index |
| Prepare inputs and questions | [State](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/state.md), [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives.md), then the chosen primitive's page |
| Decide how to handle uncertainty | [Confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence.md) |
| Write API code | [HTTP API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/api.md), [Python SDK](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/python.md), or [JavaScript SDK](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/javascript.md) |
| Update an older integration | [Migration guide](https://docs.typesafe.ai/migrating-to-v1.md) and the installed SDK's current reference |

## Find the useful shape

Start from the behavior the user wants: what will the application show, select,
change, or hand off? Work backward to the judgments it needs. Keep known rules,
calculations, exact lookups, and execution in code. Preserve the user's chosen stack
and scope; add TypeSafe where semantic understanding helps.

When brainstorming or choosing an architecture, consider more than classification.
The patterns below are starting points: combine primitives around the user's goal,
including ideas that do not fit an established recipe.

- **Route and fill known arguments.** A request can select a handler and its typed
  parameters. Ask useful branch-specific questions up front and consume only the
  relevant answers. Explore [function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md)
  and [speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md).
- **Select instead of generate.** Find candidate values or source spans in code,
  use a judgment to select the intended one, then copy or normalize it. Code can
  also assemble source text into a formatted document or reading guide. Explore
  [value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md)
  and [structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md).
- **Find and judge evidence.** Retrieve candidates, compare their relevance to a
  query, and select useful context. Explore [reranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md)
  and [hierarchical classification](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/hierarchical_classification.md).
- **Turn judgments into reusable data.** Score dimensions once, then let code or
  user controls change weights, thresholds, rankings, and views. With labeled
  outcomes, those signals can become classical ML features. Explore
  [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) and
  [feature discovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery.md).
- **Verify and escalate.** Check specific claims or fields against their evidence;
  send uncertain or failing cases to a person or reasoning model. Explore
  [citation checks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md) and
  [extraction cascades](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md).
- **Respond to changing state.** Code can retain goals and observations while fresh
  judgments guide the next bounded step. Keep inferred state distinct from observed
  facts, and check freshness before applying a result to a changed situation.

For open-ended requests, offer the few directions that best serve the user's goal
and recommend a starting point. For a concrete request, choose the relevant pattern
and build; a brainstorm is not a mandatory detour.

## Design the judgments

Choose by what the answer means, then read the relevant primitive page:

| Need | Primitive | Important distinction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One of a defined set | [Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice.md) | Picks one option; its distribution compares competing options |
| Whether a condition holds | [Noul](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/noul.md) | Probability of yes; no separate confidence; use one per label when several may apply |
| Degree along a described dimension | [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md) | Probability-weighted position on ordered levels; use comparable per-item Scores for graded ranking |

Give each question enough relevant **state** to answer: source text, identities,
relationships, policies, and current facts. Prefer named JSON fields when context
has several parts. Put the judgment in **instructions** and define its possible
answers in **criteria**. Question IDs are for code and are not sent to the model;
include complete meaning in the question. Reference nested state with backticked
paths such as `ticket.messages[0].text`.

Ask one narrow, coherent judgment per question. Split independently useful dimensions,
without destroying the relationship being judged. A bounded action selection or
contextual interpretation is valid; atomic does not mean literal fact extraction
or a one-sentence limit. Strings work for simple questions. Use structured objects
or arrays when definitions, contrasts, exclusions, or examples clarify instructions
or criteria. Score levels must describe concrete situations and stand on their own.

Keep the needed answers available. Include a no-match outcome when nothing may fit;
use a separate presence judgment when it is independently useful. For source-value
selection, check candidate coverage: the model cannot choose an omitted value.

## Compose and verify

**Ask independent questions over the same state together**, including useful
speculative questions. They run in parallel and cannot see one another's answers.
State each speculative premise explicitly; code consumes the applicable answers.
A second request is warranted when an earlier answer is needed to fetch evidence,
construct new state, or determine the next options. Extra questions still use tokens;
measure actual request budgets, cost, and end-to-end latency.

Use probabilities and confidence to guide behavior, with thresholds evaluated on
the user's data and consequences. Choice/Score confidence summarizes distribution
concentration, not overall workflow correctness or permission to act. A Noul near
0.5 means similar probability for yes and no, not medium intensity. Several
acceptable alternatives can also spread probability; low confidence need not
invalidate a harmless preference choice. Ignore uncertainty on unused branches.

Keep policy explicit and raw judgments reusable. Weighted scores suit compensating
preferences; an “any serious violation” rule needs separate conditions. Changing a
weight or display filter need not rerun inference when evidence and question meanings
are unchanged. Typed output guarantees the interface, not truth. System One models
are trained for calibrated decisions; validate their performance in the target domain.

Test representative cases and the resulting application behavior. For failures,
inspect the exact state, questions, candidates, answers, composition, and observed
outcome. Separate missing evidence, model errors, code errors, and service failures.
Treat cookbook thresholds and demo results as examples to evaluate, not universal
rules or permanent model limitations. Keep API credentials server-side in web apps.

# Example use cases

> Explore TypeSafe use cases by industry and turn promising ideas into software workflows.

Use this map to brainstorm where TypeSafe could fit in your industry. Open the closest industry, scan the example decisions, and adapt them to the documents and actions in your own workflow.

## Example use case categories

> **AI Automation Software**
>
> Interleave AI with reliable software in a way where you can run it a million times in the background without a human co-pilot. Code owns control flow (not markdown files) while TypeSafe handles the semantic decisions and language understanding.

> **Real-time applications**
>
> Frontier intelligence at real-time speeds (150ms) means AI can make decisions faster than human perception. Fast and smart enough to be programmed to play games or embedded into a UI.

> **AI Map Reduce over Big Data**
>
> 100x cheaper means you can process giant datasets. Search for relevant information over giant corpuses, classify giant agent traces, and extract features to make predictions.

> **Universal Verification**
>
> Verify the input prompt, extractions, reasoning traces, tool calls, or inputs of any other AI. Detect jailbreaks, citation errors, hallucinations, mistakes, or other error-modes that other AIs or LLMs make at a fraction of the cost for the actual LLM call.

> **Harness Engineering**
>
> Use Jev queries to make your harness smarter - model routing, semantic context retrieval, LLM error detection and guardrails, reasoning trace classification at lightspeed and a fraction of the cost.

## Example automation use cases

content.content:
## Limits and failure modes

Hard limits (`jev-1.13`, verified on the Models page):

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Price | $0.042 per million input tokens. Output tokens free. |
| Context | 64k per request; 32k for `state` plus the longest question |
| Choice options | 255 maximum, roughly 240 before reliability drops |
| Score levels | 2 minimum, 10 maximum. An 11th returns a server error. |
| Input | Text only. String, JSON object, or array. No image, audio, video. |
| Rate | 250,000 tokens/sec, 1,200 requests/min, adjusted without notice |
| Latency | About 100 to 115 ms per call, measured across two cookbooks |
| Language | English is best. Other languages accepted, lower accuracy. |

Documented failure modes, from the jev-1.13 jaggedness page:

1. **Not a calculator.** Counting, arithmetic, and comparing numeric representations
   are all unreliable. Keep math in code.
2. **Dates are read as text, not ordered quantities.** It cannot reliably tell which
   date is earlier or whether one falls in a window. Extract the parts as Choices over
   enumerated options, assemble and compare in code.
3. **Literal reading.** It answers the question you wrote, not the one you meant. If
   you find yourself explaining what you really meant, that explanation is the missing
   half of the instruction.
4. **Context rot.** Accuracy falls as the state grows with irrelevant content. Filter
   in code first, send only what the question needs.
5. **Not adversarial by default.** State is data, and injected instructions can move
   the answer. Never a security boundary on its own.
6. **No structural invariants.** A Noul and an equivalent yes/no Choice are different
   questions and give different numbers. P(A) and 1 - P(not A) do not have to agree;
   one measured pair summed to 1.19. Never carry a threshold tuned on one primitive
   over to another.
7. **Consistent but not deterministic.** Mean run-to-run probability standard deviation
   is 0.0102, far tighter than any LLM tested, but labels near a threshold still flip:
   2 of 8 questions changed their top label across 15 repeats. The fix is an explicit
   uncertain band (Noul 0.30 to 0.70, Choice top probability under 0.60) routed to a
   person, which took label agreement to 99.2% while still auto-deciding 74.2%.

## Where it fits what we run

Governance tier controls everything, because Jev is a cloud API and Baylor data rules
apply. **A** = no athlete or health data leaves the machine. **B** = possible only
after de-identification. **C** = blocked without IT approval.

| Cookbook / pattern | Our workflow | Primitive sketch | Tier | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `skill_suggestion` | Pick 1 skill from ~155 for each prompt | Choice over all skills + 3 Noul gates, then rerank top 3 | A | S |
| `classification_using_confidence` | Tag Zotero papers by topic; report a broader topic when unsure instead of dropping | 1 Choice over the taxonomy, back off one level below 0.9 confidence | A | S |
| `rerank_typesafe` | memsearch result quality | 1 Noul per query-candidate pair, sort by noul | A | S |
| `classifying_rag_passages` | Filter what reaches a prompt from memsearch or the vault | 4 Nouls: relevant, has evidence, contradicts premise, injection | A | M |
| `entity_alignment` | Athlete ID reconciliation across Catapult, VALD, Perch, S2, roster | 1 Score with 3 levels (different / curator / same) + 1 Noul per field | B | M |
| `composite-scoring` | Project registry ranking, prioritization slate | 1 Score per dimension, weights in code | A | S |
| `semantic_find` | Query the NCAA charter, policies, contracts by plain question | Choice over tagged line IDs + Noul "does an answer exist" | A | S |
| `citation_check` | Verify the Research in 5 deck and status report before sending | String-match the quote in code, then 1 Choice: supports / contradicts / says nothing | A | M |
| `sde_cascade` | Verify Claude's own extractions before they land in STATUS.md or the vault | 1 Noul per field framed so true means escalate, gate on max | A | M |
| `autoresearch_feature_discovery` | Turn free-text notes into numeric model features | Score + Noul per feature, answers become CatBoost columns | B/C | L |
| `function_calling` | Natural language to our own CLIs (`portfolio.py`, report commands) | 1 Choice over commands + 1 Choice per closed-set argument + a `stated` Noul | A | M |
| `hierarchical_classification` | Deep taxonomy walks (CPC-style research trees) | 1 Choice per level, beam search over probabilities | A | L |
| `llm_guardrails` | Screen anything scraped or pasted before an agent acts on it | Noul battery + severity Score, thresholds per policy | A | M |
| `autoresearch_feature_discovery` | PP_Recruiting pre-portal screening | 20 to 30 narrow Nouls and Scores per scouting note, answers join the percentile matrix as columns | A, see note | L |

### PP_Recruiting: not now, and what would change that

Assessed 2026-09-19 against the 009 workbook and the 09-16 validation run. **Nothing
here is worth building today.** Recording it so it does not get re-litigated.

The screening engine itself is out of scope permanently: it compares percentiles to
thresholds (75th percentile, 0.375 elite share, Impact 90+), which is the exact thing
the jaggedness page says Jev is unreliable at. Its real weakness is calibration, not
judgment quality. The 09-16 validation ran low by 0.77 tiers on average, 1.25 against
Power Four, and caught 5 of 15 defensive players. That is fixed by more graded
validation players and code, not by a different model.

Two candidates that looked like fits and are not:

- **Player entity resolution.** Collapses to a code join. Telemetry carries a stable
  `PlayerId`, and `load_leaderboard.py` already joins Player Traits to Advanced Stats
  on it. The one open cross-source question (Jordan Church) is a single name against
  the recap list, and 30 of 30 transfers already matched by hand. One player is not a
  pattern.
- **Role assignment (WR/SLOT, END/JACK, CB/STAR).** The live blocker on deliverable
## Where not to use it

- **Numeric verification on its own.** Correcting my 09-19 chat answer: the citation
  pipeline does apply to the TOS brief, but the part that catches a misquoted number is
  the **code string-match in step 1**, not Jev. Jev's Choice catches "this section says

Hard limits (`jev-1.13`, verified on the Models page):

|---|---|

content.text:
# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.

# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.

The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:

# verifier

Checks a Research in 5 deck against the paper it reports, before it is sent. Numbers
are matched in code; prose is judged by one Jev Choice per claim against the page the
deck cites. The deck's verdict is the worst single claim, so one red flag survives
rather than being averaged away.

Since 2026-09-20, figures written **inside prose** also get a code check before the
model is called — it can only escalate to `fabricated`, never settle to `verified`,
because "this integer is somewhere in the paper" is nearly meaningless when the
bibliography is full of digits. Catches 5 of 6 planted fabrications with 0 false
alarms. The blind spot is small integers; see `../docs/DELIVERABLE_VERIFIER.md`.

Tier A: a published paper and a deck about it. No athlete data.

```bash
python claims.py <review.json>              # what would be checked, and how
python verify.py --review <review.json>     # the check; exits 1 on anything real
python verify.py --review <review.json> --json
python verify.py --selftest                 # prose numeric pre-check, 10 cases, FREE
python test_verify.py                       # real deck + five planted defects
python calibrate.py                         # sweep AUTO_ACCEPT over saved answers, free
python calibrate.py --collect               # re-pay for the 38 calls, rewrites runs/
```

`calibrate.py` is the hand-labelled calibration of the `AUTO_ACCEPT` confidence floor:
17 real prose claims plus 21 planted defects, labelled against **the page the code
pairs the claim with** rather than against the paper. Answers are cached in
`runs/calibration.jsonl`, so the sweep is offline and costs nothing; only `--collect`
calls the API.

The measured answer is that **0.80 stays**, on margin rather than on defect count: the
zero-defect floor is 0.60, but the worst wrong `supports` on a planted defect scored
0.58, so 0.60 clears it by 0.02 and 0.80 by 0.22. Do not lower it without re-running
the sweep. The full table, the rule amendment that decision rests on, and the finding
that the model *endorses* fabricated figures in prose at 0.38–0.58, are in
`../docs/DELIVERABLE_VERIFIER.md`.

Needs `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` (env or `~/.claude/typesafe.env`, keeping its `apikey_`
prefix) and the zotero-research bridge index for the source paper's page text. A paper
synced without `include_fulltext` has no page text and the verifier says so rather
than guessing.

Design, measurements, what is deliberately not checked, and the false-alarm bug that
shaped the numeric matcher: `../docs/DELIVERABLE_VERIFIER.md`.

`characterisation.py` checks words that characterise a figure ("doubles", "half of",
"most of") against the figures in the same block. Pure code, no API calls, no key
needed. It is a guard with no live target today: the TOS brief does not print the
measurements it characterises, and the Research in 5 decks use no characterising words
at all. See `../docs/DELIVERABLE_VERIFIER.md`.

    python characterisation.py <file.md>
    python characterisation.py --selftest      # 13 cases, incl. defects planted in real prose

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Check a markdown evidence brief against the evidence it presents for itself.

The Research in 5 verifier checks a deck against the source paper. That is not
possible for the TOS evidence brief: it draws on 109 sources fetched from PubMed,
and none of the three papers behind its known errors are in the Zotero library, so
there is no source text to check against. Verified, not assumed - searched by author,
DOI and title, zero hits.

But this brief does something the deck does not: **it presents its own evidence next
to its own conclusions.** A section states the numbers, cites them, and then draws a
claim beneath. That makes a different and still useful question available:

    does the evidence in this section support the claim made in this section?

Which is precisely the failure mode Codex named in it - *"the central concern is not
fabricated literature ... the risk comes from the final inferential step"*. Descriptive
findings over-converted into causal, actionable claims.

What this CANNOT catch, and the limit is worth stating plainly: an error that is
faithful to the brief's own summary but unfaithful to the paper behind it. If the
brief misreports what a study found and then reasons correctly from that
misreport, the section is internally consistent and this check passes it. Only the
source paper settles that, and for this brief the source papers are not available.

    python verify_brief.py --brief <path.md>
    python verify_brief.py --brief <path.md> --json
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import re
import sys
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "zotero_classify"))

content.content:
# video_check

Pre-registered test: can Jev flag unsupported claims in a video summary?
Spec and bars: `../docs/VIDEO_SUMMARY_CHECK_PREREG.md` (bars PROPOSED until Eric approves).

- `build_sample.py` : builds `sample.csv` from `../../42Analytics/videos/*` (no model calls).
- `sample.csv` : 100 rows now (60 real, 20 wrong_locator, 20 cross_video). 40 authored plants
  (negation, mechanism) go in `authored_plants.csv` before any call, then rerun the builder.
- Next: answer key for the 60 real rows, then Eric approves bars, then calls (Mac).
-----
# Video summary claim check: pre-registration

Eleventh item measured against the capability map. Drafted 2026-09-30, **before any
model call**. **Status: bars PROPOSED, not yet approved by Eric.** No Jev call runs until
Eric approves the bars below and the answer key is committed. The registering commit is
the one that adds this file; the approval is a second commit that changes this line.
Consumer: `erash11/42Analytics` (video summaries) and through it `erash11/Flint`.

This is the test the 2026-09-26 STATUS entry left open: "Jev checking course summaries
against their transcripts, only if someone other than Eric reads those summaries."
Flint reads these summaries and ingests them into the knowledge base Eric uses, so the
condition is met. Eric's call whether it counts.

**Governance: tier A.** The state is public conference transcripts (YouTube
auto-captions) and Claude-written summaries of them. No athlete data, no health records,
no Baylor data. `applications.md` files (which quote Eric's method baseline) are not in
scope and never sent.

## Question

Can Jev tell, from a short transcript passage, whether a one-sentence claim in a video
summary is supported by that passage, well enough that 42Analytics can flag unsupported
claims before they reach Flint?

## Gate check (capability map, three conditions)

1. **Genuinely fuzzy.** A summary claim is a paraphrase. "Does this passage say that?" is
   not a join, threshold or lookup.
2. **A consumer exists.** Flint's review gate requires that nothing reaches the vault
   without a falsify pass. Today that is a Codex or Opus read of every entry.
3. **Code baseline measured first.** Numbers and time locators are checked in code
   (`42Analytics/scripts/check_summary.py`, run on 10 summaries: 0 locators past the end
   of a transcript, 0 far from a marker, 5 of ~190 numbers not found). Jev sees neither
   numbers nor locators. It sees prose only, matching the verifier's rule.

## Design (copied from `verifier/`, the Research in 5 checker)

- Deterministic extraction of claims in code: bullets under "## Key claims" with a
  locator.
- The passage is chosen in code from the cited locators (plus or minus 45 seconds,
  capped at 3,000 characters). Jev never receives the whole transcript.
- Planted defects are the real evidence. A checker that always says "supported" would
  score well on real summaries.

## Sample (`video_check/sample.csv`, built by `video_check/build_sample.py`, seed 20260930)

| Kind | n | Expected | How it is made |
|---|---|---|---|
| real | 60 | unknown, fixed by the answer key | 6 per video from the 10 pilot summaries |
| wrong_locator | 20 | not supported | a real claim with a passage 8 or more minutes from its cited time |
| cross_video | 20 | not supported | a real claim with a passage from a different talk |
| negation | 20 | contradicted | Claude rewrites a real claim to say the opposite (authored file, committed before any call) |
| mechanism | 20 | not supported | Claude adds a plausible reason or detail the speaker never gave, the failure Flint's reviews found most often (authored file) |

Total 140. The claims come from Sonnet-written summaries. The passages come from
captions Claude did not write. The authored plants are written once, before any call.

## Answer key

Claude (a different model instance from the summarizer, blind to every Jev answer)
labels each of the 60 real items **supported / partly / not supported** from the same
passage, and commits the labels before the first Jev call. Planted items carry their
label by construction. A real claim labelled "partly" or "not supported" is itself a
finding about the summaries.

## Questions (per item, same state for every model)

State: `claim` and `passage`. Instructions forbid judging from outside knowledge.

1. **Support.** Noul: does the passage say or directly imply the claim?
2. **Contradiction.** Noul: does the passage say the opposite of the claim?
3. **Extra detail.** Noul: does the claim include a specific detail (a reason, name, cause
   or mechanism) that the passage does not contain?

Aggregation, following `sde_cascade`: an item is **flagged** if Q2 or Q3 is at or above
the cut, or Q1 is at or below 1 minus the cut. Cut: 0.50, the measured value elsewhere
in this project, fixed here.

## Comparators (same 140, same state)

- Haiku: one call per item, forced to answer supported / partly / not supported.
- Codex: the same.
- Claude's own pass is the answer key, so it is not a comparator.

## Bars (PROPOSED, fixed on approval, they never move)

| Measure | Bar |
|---|---|
| Jev decisive: not in the 0.35 to 0.65 band on all three questions | at least 60% of the 140 |
| Catch rate on planted items (flagged / 80), decisive items only | at least 85% overall and at least 75% in each of the four kinds |
| False alarm rate on real items the key labels "supported" | at most 10% |
| Jev versus Haiku: catch rate at equal or lower false alarm rate | Jev at least equal |
| Cost for the 140 items | reported, no bar |

The 0.35 to 0.65 band and the 10% false-alarm bar are my proposal. Eric may change
either before approval.

## Answer-key audit (required step)

Per `JEV_CAPABILITY_MAP.md`: pull Jev's confident disagreements with the labels (cap 20,
random 20 if more), Eric judges them blind (label right, Jev right, unclear), and both
scores are reported. The original labels decide pass or fail.

## What each outcome changes

- **Pass:** add a Jev pre-screen to the summary pipeline: unflagged claims skip the
  expensive falsify read, flagged ones go to it. Numbers stay in code.
- **Fail:** record which kind failed and keep the Codex or Opus read as the only gate.

## Not measured here

Whether summaries capture a talk's main points (omissions); whether the auto-captions are
accurate; "Eric's baseline:" attributions (those need `method-baseline.md`, not a
transcript).

## Runtime notes

Pre-registered test: can Jev flag unsupported claims in a video summary?
Spec and bars: `../docs/VIDEO_SUMMARY_CHECK_PREREG.md` (bars PROPOSED until Eric approves).

- `build_sample.py` : builds `sample.csv` from `../../42Analytics/videos/*` (no model calls).
- `sample.csv` : 100 rows now (60 real, 20 wrong_locator, 20 cross_video). 40 authored plants
  (negation, mechanism) go in `authored_plants.csv` before any call, then rerun the builder.
- Next: answer key for the 60 real rows, then Eric approves bars, then calls (Mac).
-----
# Video summary claim check: pre-registration

Eleventh item measured against the capability map. Drafted 2026-09-30, **before any
model call**. **Status: bars PROPOSED, not yet approved by Eric.** No Jev call runs until
Eric approves the bars below and the answer key is committed. The registering commit is
the one that adds this file; the approval is a second commit that changes this line.
Consumer: `erash11/42Analytics` (video summaries) and through it `erash11/Flint`.

This is the test the 2026-09-26 STATUS entry left open: "Jev checking course summaries
against their transcripts, only if someone other than Eric reads those summaries."
Flint reads these summaries and ingests them into the knowledge base Eric uses, so the
condition is met. Eric's call whether it counts.

**Governance: tier A.** The state is public conference transcripts (YouTube
auto-captions) and Claude-written summaries of them. No athlete data, no health records,
no Baylor data. `applications.md` files (which quote Eric's method baseline) are not in
scope and never sent.

## Question

Can Jev tell, from a short transcript passage, whether a one-sentence claim in a video
summary is supported by that passage, well enough that 42Analytics can flag unsupported
claims before they reach Flint?

## Gate check (capability map, three conditions)

1. **Genuinely fuzzy.** A summary claim is a paraphrase. "Does this passage say that?" is
   not a join, threshold or lookup.
2. **A consumer exists.** Flint's review gate requires that nothing reaches the vault
   without a falsify pass. Today that is a Codex or Opus read of every entry.
3. **Code baseline measured first.** Numbers and time locators are checked in code
   (`42Analytics/scripts/check_summary.py`, run on 10 summaries: 0 locators past the end
   of a transcript, 0 far from a marker, 5 of ~190 numbers not found). Jev sees neither
   numbers nor locators. It sees prose only, matching the verifier's rule.

## Design (copied from `verifier/`, the Research in 5 checker)

- Deterministic extraction of claims in code: bullets under "## Key claims" with a
  locator.
- The passage is chosen in code from the cited locators (plus or minus 45 seconds,
  capped at 3,000 characters). Jev never receives the whole transcript.
- Planted defects are the real evidence. A checker that always says "supported" would
  score well on real summaries.

## Sample (`video_check/sample.csv`, built by `video_check/build_sample.py`, seed 20260930)

| Kind | n | Expected | How it is made |
|---|---|---|---|
| real | 60 | unknown, fixed by the answer key | 6 per video from the 10 pilot summaries |
| wrong_locator | 20 | not supported | a real claim with a passage 8 or more minutes from its cited time |
| cross_video | 20 | not supported | a real claim with a passage from a different talk |
| negation | 20 | contradicted | Claude rewrites a real claim to say the opposite (authored file, committed before any call) |
| mechanism | 20 | not supported | Claude adds a plausible reason or detail the speaker never gave, the failure Flint's reviews found most often (authored file) |

Total 140. The claims come from Sonnet-written summaries. The passages come from
captions Claude did not write. The authored plants are written once, before any call.

## Answer key

Claude (a different model instance from the summarizer, blind to every Jev answer)
labels each of the 60 real items **supported / partly / not supported** from the same
passage, and commits the labels before the first Jev call. Planted items carry their
label by construction. A real claim labelled "partly" or "not supported" is itself a
finding about the summaries.

## Questions (per item, same state for every model)

State: `claim` and `passage`. Instructions forbid judging from outside knowledge.

1. **Support.** Noul: does the passage say or directly imply the claim?
2. **Contradiction.** Noul: does the passage say the opposite of the claim?
3. **Extra detail.** Noul: does the claim include a specific detail (a reason, name, cause
   or mechanism) that the passage does not contain?

Aggregation, following `sde_cascade`: an item is **flagged** if Q2 or Q3 is at or above
the cut, or Q1 is at or below 1 minus the cut. Cut: 0.50, the measured value elsewhere
in this project, fixed here.

## Comparators (same 140, same state)

- Haiku: one call per item, forced to answer supported / partly / not supported.
- Codex: the same.
- Claude's own pass is the answer key, so it is not a comparator.

## Bars (PROPOSED, fixed on approval, they never move)

| Measure | Bar |
|---|---|
| Jev decisive: not in the 0.35 to 0.65 band on all three questions | at least 60% of the 140 |
| Catch rate on planted items (flagged / 80), decisive items only | at least 85% overall and at least 75% in each of the four kinds |
| False alarm rate on real items the key labels "supported" | at most 10% |
| Jev versus Haiku: catch rate at equal or lower false alarm rate | Jev at least equal |
| Cost for the 140 items | reported, no bar |

The 0.35 to 0.65 band and the 10% false-alarm bar are my proposal. Eric may change
either before approval.

## Answer-key audit (required step)

Per `JEV_CAPABILITY_MAP.md`: pull Jev's confident disagreements with the labels (cap 20,
random 20 if more), Eric judges them blind (label right, Jev right, unclear), and both
scores are reported. The original labels decide pass or fail.

## What each outcome changes

- **Pass:** add a Jev pre-screen to the summary pipeline: unflagged claims skip the
  expensive falsify read, flagged ones go to it. Numbers stay in code.
- **Fail:** record which kind failed and keep the Codex or Opus read as the only gate.

## Not measured here

Whether summaries capture a talk's main points (omissions); whether the auto-captions are
accurate; "Eric's baseline:" attributions (those need `method-baseline.md`, not a
transcript).

## Runtime notes

Calls need `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` and `typesafe-sdk`. On 2026-09-30 neither was present on
the Windows laptop, so the calls run on the Mac (key in Keychain). The sample and
answer key can be built on either machine.

operational instruction file and takes precedence for build details.

## What it is

"The Monitor" is a biweekly internal newsletter communicating the Applied Performance
department's work, methods, and value.

Audience is mixed: coaches, athletic administrators, and support staff. Not uniformly
technical, and that shapes every writing decision here.

## People

Eric Rash (Director of Applied Performance). Kenny Boyd is supervisor. Blake Wright is
the embedded PhD student leading B.A.I.R. research. Chris Ruf, Danny Davis, and
Dr. Andrew Gallucci are regular figures.

B.A.I.R. bridges Baylor's R1 research mission with athletic performance support across
14 varsity sports.

## Voice and attribution

Written in department voice ("we"). Signed "Baylor Applied Performance / B.A.I.R.
Initiative", never under Eric's name personally.

This was a deliberate correction: early drafts in first person were rejected, and "we"
is now the established standard.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Comparators for the Drive triage pilot: one call per file, forced to name a topic.

    python drive_triage/run_llm.py haiku          # headless `claude -p` on Haiku 4.5
    python drive_triage/run_llm.py codex          # `codex exec`
    python drive_triage/run_llm.py haiku --limit 1

Same state (private/state.jsonl), same 96 topics and six routes as Jev. The model answers
with JSON {"topic": ..., "route": ...}; anything outside the vocabulary is recorded as a
failure, not coerced. Resumable: rows already in runs/<name>.jsonl are skipped.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import re
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from pathlib import Path

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(HERE.parent / "zotero_classify"))
sys.path.insert(0, str(HERE))
import classify  # noqa: E402
import taxonomy  # noqa: E402
from run_jev import ROUTES  # noqa: E402

SYSTEM = (
    "You classify one Drive file for a sport-science knowledge base. You get a JSON "
    "object with the file's folder, file_name, and sometimes zotero_title and first_page. "
    "Answer two questions from that evidence only.\n\n"
    "1. topic: " + classify.QUESTION + " Always pick exactly one topic name from this list, "
    "even when the evidence is thin:\n"
    + "\n".join(f"- {t}: {c}" for t, c in taxonomy.CRITERIA.items())
    + "\n\n2. route: pick exactly one of:\n"
    + "\n".join(f"- {r}: {c}" for r, c in ROUTES.items())
    + "\n\nThe evidence you are given is all there is. Never ask for more and never refuse: "
    "when it is thin, give the most probable answer.\n"
    + 'Reply with ONLY a JSON object: {"topic": "<topic name>", "route": "<route>"}'
)
USER_SUFFIX = '\n\nAnswer now with only the JSON object {"topic": ..., "route": ...}.'


def call(name: str, state: dict) -> str:
    prompt = json.dumps(state, ensure_ascii=False) + USER_SUFFIX
    if name == "haiku":
        exe = shutil.which("claude.exe") or shutil.which("claude.cmd") or shutil.which("claude") or "claude"
        cmd = [exe, "-p", "--model", "claude-haiku-4-5", "--tools", "",
               "--system-prompt", SYSTEM, "--output-format", "text"]
        stdin = prompt
    else:
        exe = shutil.which("codex.cmd") or shutil.which("codex") or "codex"
        cmd = [exe, "exec", "--skip-git-repo-check", "--sandbox", "read-only", "-"]
        stdin = SYSTEM + "\n\nFile:\n" + prompt
    p = subprocess.run(cmd, input=stdin, capture_output=True, text=True, encoding="utf-8",
                       errors="replace", timeout=300, cwd=str(HERE / "private"))
    return p.stdout


def parse(text: str) -> dict:
    found = re.findall(r"\{[^{}]*\"topic\"[^{}]*\}", text, re.S)
    if not found:
        raise ValueError("no JSON answer")
    d = json.loads(found[-1])
    if d.get("topic") not in taxonomy.DOMAIN_OF:
        raise ValueError(f"topic outside taxonomy: {d.get('topic')!r}")
    if d.get("route") not in ROUTES:
        raise ValueError(f"route outside the six: {d.get('route')!r}")
    return d


def main() -> int:
    name = sys.argv[1]
    limit = int(sys.argv[sys.argv.index("--limit") + 1]) if "--limit" in sys.argv else 0
    workers = int(sys.argv[sys.argv.index("--workers") + 1]) if "--workers" in sys.argv else 2
    state = [json.loads(l) for l in (HERE / "private" / "state.jsonl").read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines() if l.strip()]
    out = HERE / "runs" / f"{name}.jsonl"
    out.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import re
import shutil
import subprocess

import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from pathlib import Path

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent

sys.path.insert(0, str(HERE))
import classify  # noqa: E402
import taxonomy  # noqa: E402
from run_jev import ROUTES  # noqa: E402

SYSTEM = (
    "You classify one Drive file for a sport-science knowledge base. You get a JSON "
    "object with the file's folder, file_name, and sometimes zotero_title and first_page. "
    "Answer two questions from that evidence only.\n\n"
    "1. topic: " + classify.QUESTION + " Always pick exactly one topic name from this list, "
    "even when the evidence is thin:\n"
    + "\n".join(f"- {t}: {c}" for t, c in taxonomy.CRITERIA.items())
    + "\n\n2. route: pick exactly one of:\n"
    + "\n".join(f"- {r}: {c}" for r, c in ROUTES.items())
    + "\n\nThe evidence you are given is all there is. Never ask for more and never refuse: "
    "when it is thin, give the most probable answer.\n"
    + 'Reply with ONLY a JSON object: {"topic": "<topic name>", "route": "<route>"}'
)
USER_SUFFIX = '\n\nAnswer now with only the JSON object {"topic": ..., "route": ...}.'


def call(name: str, state: dict) -> str:
    prompt = json.dumps(state, ensure_ascii=False) + USER_SUFFIX
    if name == "haiku":
        exe = shutil.which("claude.exe") or shutil.which("claude.cmd") or shutil.which("claude") or "claude"
        cmd = [exe, "-p", "--model", "claude-haiku-4-5", "--tools", "",
               "--system-prompt", SYSTEM, "--output-format", "text"]
        stdin = prompt
    else:
        exe = shutil.which("codex.cmd") or shutil.which("codex") or "codex"
        cmd = [exe, "exec", "--skip-git-repo-check", "--sandbox", "read-only", "-"]
        stdin = SYSTEM + "\n\nFile:\n" + prompt
    p = subprocess.run(cmd, input=stdin, capture_output=True, text=True, encoding="utf-8",
                       errors="replace", timeout=300, cwd=str(HERE / "private"))

def parse(text: str) -> dict:
    found = re.findall(r"\{[^{}]*\"topic\"[^{}]*\}", text, re.S)

    state = [json.loads(l) for l in (HERE / "private" / "state.jsonl").read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines() if l.strip()]

and brand. Nothing from Clemson or Iowa is quoted into Digest chapters.

- Path: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\99_UNSORTED\From_External\Performance Play Book\Baylor Applied Performance Playbook.docx`

Performance mission and four operating principles, technology overview (11 entries), login

# Chapter 1: ForceDecks countermovement jump procedure

**DRAFT 0.2, 2026-10-06. Not yet run by a named user. Items marked [CONFIRM: ...] are
Baylor facts the author could not verify. Do not ship until they are resolved.**

Part 2, Ops manual. Applied Performance Digest.

| Owner | Daily user | Last reviewed |
|---|---|---|
| Director of Applied Performance | [CONFIRM: name and role of the staff member or intern who runs CMJ testing most days] | 2026-10-04 (draft) |

## The short version

Two countermovement jumps on the ForceDecks, hands on hips, after a weigh-in that reads
green. The athlete stands still, bends, jumps as high as they can, sticks a stiff athletic
landing, and resets. You review the two reps before you save. The whole thing takes
[CONFIRM: time per athlete] once the plates are up.

## What this test is for

The countermovement jump (CMJ) is the test Applied Performance runs most, and it does three
jobs:

1. Daily readiness. Jumps during the week build each athlete's baseline. Modified
   reactive strength index (RSI-modified) is read against that baseline on Wednesdays, using
   percent change, a rolling average, and the smallest worthwhile change to tell a real drop
   from noise. Thresholds are individual, not one number for the team.
2. Asymmetry. Left and right plate forces show whether an athlete is loading one side
   more than the other. Useful monthly, and more often for an athlete returning from injury
   with Athletic Medicine.
3. Training emphasis. CMJ peak force divided by isometric mid-thigh pull peak force
   gives the dynamic strength index, which helps decide between more plyometric work and
   more maximal strength work. That needs the mid-thigh pull too; see chapter O5.

Because the same test serves three purposes, the procedure has to be the same every time.
A test can keep its name while the cue, the rep count or a software setting changes
underneath it, and the data will not tell you. That is why this chapter fixes all three in
writing.

How often: daily or near-daily during training blocks for the readiness baseline
[CONFIRM: which sports jump daily, and which jump weekly]. Monthly asymmetry review.
Before and after a training phase for the dynamic strength index.

What we report: pick a few metrics and keep them. The working rule is one or two output
metrics (jump height), one to three driver metrics (concentric impulse, eccentric braking
force), one to three strategy metrics (contraction time, countermovement depth), and
left-right asymmetry where it matters. Add anything else only with a reason written down.
[CONFIRM: the current reported metric set for daily readiness and for coach reports.]

### Equipment

1. ForceDecks dual force plates [CONFIRM: model, serial numbers]
2. Laptop or tablet with the ForceDecks app, version 2.1 (latest) [CONFIRM: device name; check the version number on the device's About screen]
3. Plate cables and power supply
4. Carrying case [CONFIRM: storage location, room and shelf]

content.content:
## The characterisation check: built, and the premise above was wrong

`verifier/characterisation.py`, 2026-09-19. Pure code, no API calls. It extracts every
characterising word ("doubles", "half of", "most of", "an order of magnitude") and
checks it against the figures in the same block.

**It works, and it has no live target.** Both statements are measured:

- **The TOS brief never prints 14.4 or 9.4.** The section above proposed this check on
  the assumption those measurements sit next to the claim. They do not - the brief says
  "roughly doubles scalene stiffness" with no figures at all, at lines 44 and 375. The
  numbers are in the Takaba paper, which is not in Zotero. So the check correctly stays
  silent, and *structurally cannot* reach that error from this document. 19
  characterising words in the brief, only 2 with figures beside them, neither
  contradicted.
- **The Research in 5 decks contain zero characterising words.** Confirmed by grep over
  `review.json`, not inferred from a null run. The deck format is number-forward tables,
  and the numeric string match already owns those.

Of the three known TOS errors it could only ever have caught one. The other two are a
referent error ("roughly half of true pitch volume" against a 51.2% that counts outings
exceeding a recommendation, a different quantity) and an attribution question. Neither
is arithmetic. The original "what would close it" line overstated the fix.

So it ships as a **guard**: zero cost, runs in a send gate, fires the day a deliverable
describes a figure in words.

### The three false alarms it produced first, and what each taught

The first run over the real brief raised four flags. Three were false, which against
this project's zero-false-alarm bar is a failing tool. Each traced to the window rather
than the arithmetic:

| flag | cause | fix |
|---|---|---|
| `twice` at 1.22x | divided `11 / 9` out of the citation `Diagnostics (Basel) 2021;11(9):1529` | `CITATION_NOISE` strips journal volume(issue):page, PMID, DOI and `p. 6` before any figure is read |
| `most` on "the single **most** striking number" | bare "most" is usually a superlative and asserts no proportion | quantifier forms only: `most of`, `the majority of`, `half of`, `half the` |

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/project

# /project — portfolio registry skill

Drives the `project-triage` CLI to capture ideas, log progress and change
project status. The registry (`portfolio.json`) is the single source of truth.
The live board (`board.py`) is its front door and re-renders on its own within
a few seconds of any registry change, so there is nothing to render or publish.
(The static `dashboard.html`, its Artifact and `pulse.md` retired 2026-10-03.)

## Paths

- Config: `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.windows.json` on Windows; `config.macos.json` on macOS
- Repo: parent directory of `portfolio_json` in the selected platform config
- Interpreter: `python` on Windows; `python3` on macOS
- Registry: `portfolio_json` in the selected platform config
- CLI entry points: `portfolio.py` (mutations and checks), `board.py` (the board)

## CLI contract (verbatim — do not alter flags)

```
python "<project-triage-repo>/portfolio.py" add-idea "<pitch>" --source "<source>"
python "<project-triage-repo>/portfolio.py" add-update "<name>" "<note>" --next-action "<optional>"
python "<project-triage-repo>/portfolio.py" set-stage "<name>" "<stage>"
python "<project-triage-repo>/portfolio.py" set-status "<name>" active|paused|done --note "<optional>"
python "<project-triage-repo>/portfolio.py" set-receiver "<name>" "<who, or me: why>"
python "<project-triage-repo>/portfolio.py" slate-check
python "<project-triage-repo>/board.py" --background
```

- `add-idea` prints `idea captured (<N> in inbox)`.
- `add-update` prints `updated <name>` (name match is case-insensitive).
- `set-stage` prints `stage set: <name> → <stage>`. Valid stages, in ladder
  order: `idea grilled spec planned building shipped`.
- `set-status` prints `status set: <name> → <status>`. It is the board's
  Start/Park/Done: a start over the slate cap is refused, and a start begins
  the 7-day clock.
- `slate-check` loads (and so validates) the registry and prints the slate
  rules; exit 0 means a hand-edit is structurally valid.
- `board.py --background` reuses the running board or starts one, opens it,
  and prints its URL.
- Any error path prints `[error] <msg>` to stderr and exits 2, with no
  mutation to `portfolio.json`. Stop and surface the message verbatim.

## Verbs

### `idea <pitch>`
Run `add-idea "<pitch>" --source "<conversation context, ≤8 words>"`. The
source should summarize where the idea came from (e.g. "chat about GPS
vendor gaps"), not just "chat".

### `update <name> <note>`
Fuzzy-match `<name>` against the project names currently in the registry
(read `portfolio.json` first). If exactly one match, run `add-update "<name>"
"<note>"` (add `--next-action "<...>"` if the user gave one). If the match is
ambiguous or there's no close match, ask the user which project they mean
before running anything.

### `start` / `park` / `done <name>`
Fuzzy-match like `update`, then `set-status "<name>" active|paused|done`.
A start on a job/side/tool project needs a receiver within 7 days: if it has
none, ask who it is for and run `set-receiver` (never invent one).

### `rank`
Read `portfolio.json`, show the lane's active projects with their current
`rank` values, and ask for the new order. Never reorder ranks yourself —
only apply the order the user gives you. Rewrite the `rank` fields directly
with the Edit tool, then validate with `slate-check` (exit 0 = valid).
Dragging on the board does the same thing and is usually quicker.

### `promote <idea>`
Ask which lane (`job`, `side`, `system`, `knowledge`, `tool`) and for a
`next_action`. With the Edit tool: set the matching idea's `status` to
`promoted`, and append a new project entry to that lane at the next free
`rank` (max existing rank in that lane + 1). Validate with `slate-check`.

### `stage <name> <stage>`
Fuzzy-match `<name>` like `update` does. Run `set-stage "<name>" "<stage>"`.

**Shipped → harvest handoff:** when the stage being set is `shipped`, offer
once: "Want me to run /harvest on <name> to distill it into your SecondBrain
and log the shipped artifact?" On yes, invoke the `harvest` skill for that
project.

### bare `/project`
Run `board.py --background` and give the URL, then show `slate-check` output
in chat.

## After every mutation

Nothing to render: the board picks the change up on its next poll. Say what
changed in one line. Registry edits are committed by closeout as
`data: board edits <date>`; do not commit them mid-session unless asked.

## Rules

- Never reorder project ranks yourself — only apply the order the user
  gives you during `rank`.
- Never delete a project or idea without explicit confirmation.
- On any `[error] ...` output from the CLI: stop immediately and show the
  error verbatim.
- `portfolio.json` is the single source of truth; tasks live in each repo's
  `docs/STATUS.md`, which the board reads and never writes.

Project: TypeSafe_Sandbox

## What this is
A sandbox for building against the TypeSafe System One API (the Jev model), which
returns typed judgments and probabilities instead of generated text. The API key is
NOT stored in this repo; see Secrets below for where it lives on each machine.
`setup_global_key.sh` installs the macOS side once per machine. `smoke_test.py` proves
the key resolves and the API answers.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

## Secrets
- Never paste the API key into a chat session. Claude Code transcripts under
  `~/.claude/projects/*.jsonl` are tracked in the `dotclaude` repo and pushed nightly.
- Never put the key in `~/.claude/settings.json` or `settings.local.json`. Both are tracked.
- The key has one home per machine, and nothing about it syncs between them:
  - macOS: the Keychain, service name `typesafe-api-key`, installed by `setup_global_key.sh`.
  - Windows: `~/.claude/typesafe.env`, which the dotclaude whitelist auto-ignores.
- The key is 108 characters and starts with `apikey_`. Dropping that prefix returns 401.
